newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees need to boost shipyards' competitiveness.
newsitem.headline: EU sees need to boost shipyards' competitiveness.

text.p: Measures must be taken to give a sharp boost to the competitive strength of European shipbuilders, which still lag behind more efficient Japanese rivals despite tough restructuring moves, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
The European Union executive said the industry should extend cooperation and integrate more actively to take advantage of economies of scale.

"There still seems to be considerable potential. It is, of course, the primary task of industry itself to tackle this challenge," the Commission said in a discussion paper to be presented to EU industry ministers meeting on April 24.
The EU could help by setting the right framework with its industrial competitiveness policy.
The industry needed support from member states as well as the Commission to cooperate much more closely in production and marketing, design and acquisition.
"Cooperation should be among yards as well as between shipbuilders, suppliers and other related players," it said.

The European industry has long struggled to boost its competitive power, slashing its workforce by 70 percent and production capacity by 60 percent since 1976, leading to the introduction of new technology and the modernisation of yards.
The latest figures available put the industry workforce at 79,000 people in 1994.

But "although certain segments of the industry in the EU are international leaders in their fields, many shipyards are encountering severe difficulties in attaining the levels of productivity and value added needed to remain viable," it said.
Shipbuilders in Europe face a few extremely powerful groups as competitors, the EU executive said.
Up to 90 percent of production in South Korea is governed by five groups. In contrast, the European industry consists of more than 100 companies.
"European shipbuilding is fragmented, geographically dispersed and heterogeneous," the Commission paper said.
In addition, the productivity of European shipyards is 25 to 50 percent below that of Japan. Productivity in South Korea is on about the same level as in Europe but labour costs are lower.

To boost competitiveness, the promotion of research and development and innovation is crucial, the document said, noting the technological leadership of Japanese yards. "Europe's shipbuilders have to focus much more on R&D," it said.
It added that it was also vital to make full use of information and communication technologies.

The EU executive reiterated its support for a rapid entry into force of an international accord brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) to slash most state support to the shipbuilding sector.

However, this accord has not yet been ratified by the United States and the Commission said there was a need to explore different scenarios, including the option of implementing the deal without Washington.
This would "eliminate subsidies and introduce, for the first time, an anti-dumping instrument between the major shipbuilding countries of the world."

Turning to the near-term outlook for the industry, the Commission said demand for ships had recently increased due to more sea transport and the need to replace a growing part of the world fleet, which has an average age of more than 20 years.

The EU has, in recent years, been able to hold on to its market share of 20 percent in terms of volume while the two main competitors from the Far East -- Japan and South Korea -- had a combined market share of 60 percent in 1996.
But regardless of the high demand the sector expects over the next years, it faces several challenges.
"Market prices are relatively low. According to industry this is due to predatory pricing of South Korean yards," the Commission said, adding that capacity was expected to grow further.
This was leading the industry to estimate that "in 2000 the actual production will not cover more than 70 percent of available capacity."
